results.question: You receive two Visa card offers: Option A is free but charges 1.5% on every foreign transaction. Option B costs CHF 8/month but has zero foreign fees. You travel to Europe 2–3 times a year. Which do you pick and why?
results.answer: I would take Option B. I easily spend a few thousand CHF per year abroad, so 1.5% quickly exceeds CHF 96 annually. The break-even is very low, and I prefer predictable costs over hidden percentage fees. For me, the math clearly favors zero foreign fees.

results.question: Your bank sends you a message: your free debit card will be replaced by a new Visa card at CHF 5/month. You can opt out and keep a basic account. What do you do?
results.answer: I would evaluate what the CHF 5 actually gives me. If it includes insurance, cashback, or removes foreign fees, it might justify itself. If it is just a rebranding with no added value, I would opt out. I do not pay for features I do not use.

results.question: A new Visa card offers 1% cashback on all Migros and Coop purchases. The monthly fee is CHF 4. Would this change how you pay at the supermarket?
results.answer: Yes, if my monthly grocery spend is around CHF 800–1,000, that is CHF 8–10 cashback. After the CHF 4 fee, I am still net positive. That is a simple and transparent return, so I would switch my supermarket payments to that card.

results.question: Which of these would make you most likely to get a Visa card: (a) 2% cashback, (b) travel insurance included, (c) no foreign transaction fees, (d) a CHF 100 welcome bonus?
results.answer: For me, (c) and (b) are the strongest combination. I travel frequently, so foreign fees and insurance have continuous value. A 2% cashback is attractive, but only if it is simple and uncapped. A one-time bonus is nice, but not a decision driver.

results.question: You currently use Twint for almost everything. A Visa card promises the same speed but adds rewards. What would it take for you to actually switch?
results.answer: It would need to match Twint's speed and reliability with zero friction. On top of that, the rewards must be automatic and transparent — no points systems or thresholds. If I clearly see monthly net gains without changing behavior, I would switch.

results.question: Have you ever been in a situation where Twint or your debit card was not accepted? What did you do — and would a credit card have solved it?
results.answer: Yes, mainly with international bookings or smaller foreign merchants. In those cases, I used my credit card or Revolut. A credit card definitely solves those gaps, especially for travel and online payments. That is why I always keep one active.

results.question: A Visa card gives you CHF 50 welcome bonus but requires CHF 6/month for 12 months — total cost CHF 72. Is that a good deal to you?
results.answer: No, purely from a numbers perspective it is negative. I pay CHF 72 to get CHF 50, so I lose CHF 22 unless there are additional benefits. If the card also provides ongoing value, I would consider it, but the bonus alone is not compelling.

results.question: If a Visa card saved you CHF 15/month through cashback and discounts, but cost CHF 10/month in fees, would you see that as a net gain or still feel reluctant?
results.answer: That is a clear net gain of CHF 5 per month. As long as the savings are consistent and not conditional, I would accept it without hesitation. The key is reliability — I do not want to track or optimize constantly.

results.question: What is the absolute maximum monthly fee you would accept for a Visa card — and only under what conditions?
results.answer: I would go up to around CHF 25–30 per month, but only if the value clearly exceeds that. That means strong travel insurance, zero foreign fees, and at least CHF 30–40 equivalent monthly value through cashback or perks. Otherwise, it is not efficient.

results.question: If a Visa card were completely free forever but offered no rewards, would you still get one? What would be the point for you?
results.answer: Yes, but purely as a functional tool. I would use it for online payments, travel bookings, and as a backup when other methods fail. Without rewards, it would not be my primary card, but it still has utility in specific situations.
